entries.5aeff723b767526321f7319d876475b3f5a2a9e7: <div sID="gen15818" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="Isa.15" sID="Isa.15"/> <div eID="gen15818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15819" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15820" type="x-p"/> This chapter, and that which follows it, are the burden of Moab—a prophecy of some great desolation that was coming upon that country, which bordered upon this land of Israel, and had often been injurious and vexatious to it, though the Moabites were descended from Lot, Abraham's kinsman and companion, and though the Israelites, by the appointment of God, had spared them when they might both easily and justly have cut them off with their neighbours. In this chapter we have, I. Great lamentation made by the Moabites, and by the prophet himself for them, <reference osisRef="Isa.15.1-Isa.15.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. The great calamities which should occasion that lamentation and justify it, <reference osisRef="Isa.15.6-Isa.15.9">ver. 6-9</reference>.
entries.0a33ed04e4d14075cb9b646f94bbf5fea1dadf23: <div eID="gen15820" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15819" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Burden of Moab. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 725.)</title> <div sID="gen15821" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The burden of Moab. Because in the night Ar of Moab is laid waste, <hi type="italic">and</hi> brought to silence; because in the night Kir of Moab is laid waste, <hi type="italic">and</hi> brought to silence; <hi type="super">2</hi> He is gone up to Bajith, and to Dibon, the high places, to weep: Moab shall howl over Nebo, and over Medeba: on all their heads <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> baldness, <hi type="italic">and</hi> every beard cut off. <hi type="super">3</hi> In their streets they shall gird themselves with sackcloth: on the tops of their houses, and in their streets, every one shall howl, weeping abundantly. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Heshbon shall cry, and Elealeh: their voice shall be heard <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto Jahaz: therefore the armed soldiers of Moab shall cry out; his life shall be grievous unto him. <hi type="super">5</hi> My heart shall cry out for Moab; his fugitives <hi type="italic">shall flee</hi> unto Zoar, a heifer of three years old: for by the mounting up of Luhith with weeping shall they go it up; for in the way of Horonaim they shall raise up a cry of destruction. <div eID="gen15821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15822" type="x-p"/> The country of Moab was of small extent, but very fruitful. It bordered upon the lot of Reuben on the other side Jordan and upon the Dead Sea. Naomi went to sojourn there when there was a famine in Canaan. This is the country which (it is here foretold) should be wasted and grievously harassed, not quite ruined, for we find another prophecy of its ruin (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.1-Jer.48.47">Jer. xlviii.</reference>), which was accomplished by Nebuchadnezzar. This prophecy here was to be fulfilled <hi type="italic">within three years</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.14">ch. xvi. 14</reference>), and therefore was fulfilled in the devastations made of that country by the army of the Assyrians, which for many years ravaged those parts, enriching themselves with spoil and plunder. It was done either by the army of Shalmaneser, about the time of the taking of Samaria, in the fourth year of Hezekiah (as is most probable), or by the army of Sennacherib, which, ten years after, invaded Judah. We cannot suppose that the prophet went among the Moabites to preach to them this sermon; but he delivered it to his own people, 1. To show them that, though judgment begins at the house of God, it shall not end there,—that there is a providence which governs the world and all the nations of it,—and that to the God of Israel the worshippers of false gods were accountable, and liable to his judgments. 2. To give them a proof of God's care of them and jealousy for them, and to convince them that God was an enemy to their enemies, for such the Moabites had often been. 3. That the accomplishment of this prophecy now shortly (<hi type="italic">within three years</hi>) might be a confirmation of the prophet's mission and of the truth of all his other prophecies, and might encourage the faithful to depend upon them. <div eID="gen15822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15823" type="x-p"/> Now concerning Moab it is here foretold, <div eID="gen15823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15824" type="x-p"/> I. That their chief cities should be surprised and taken in a night by the enemy, probably because the inhabitants, as the men of Laish, indulged themselves in ease and luxury, and dwelt securely (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.1">v. 1</reference>): Therefore there shall be great grief, <hi type="italic">because in the night Air of Moab is laid waste and Kir of Moab,</hi> the two principal cities of that kingdom. <hi type="italic">In the night that they were taken,</hi> or sacked, <hi type="italic">Moab was cut off.</hi> The seizing of them laid the whole country open, and made all the wealth of it an easy prey to the victorious army. Note, 1. Great changes and very dismal ones may be made in a very little time. Here are two cities lost in a night, though that is the time of quietness. Let us therefore lie down as those that know not what a night may bring forth. 2. As the country feeds the cities, so the cities protect the country, and neither can say to the other, <hi type="italic">I have no need of thee.</hi> <div eID="gen15824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15825" type="x-p"/> II. That the Moabites, being hereby put into the utmost consternation imaginable, should have recourse to their idols for relief, and pour out their tears before them (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">He</hi> (that is, Moab, especially the king of Moab) <hi type="italic">has gone up to Bajith</hi> (or rather to the house or temple of Chemosh), <hi type="italic">and Dibon,</hi> the inhabitants of Dibon, <hi type="italic">have gone up to the high places,</hi> where they worshipped their idols, there to make their complaints. Note, It becomes a people in distress to seek to their God; and shall not we then thus <hi type="italic">walk in the name of the Lord our God,</hi> and call upon him in the time of trouble, before whom we shall not shed such useless profitless tears as they did before their gods? <div eID="gen15825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15826" type="x-p"/> III. That there should be the voice of universal grief all the country over. It is described here elegantly and very affectingly. Moab shall be a vale of tears—a little map of this world, <reference osisRef="Isa.15.2">v. 2</reference>. The Moabites shall lament the loss of Nebo and Medeba, two considerable cities, which, it is likely, were plundered and burnt. They shall tear their hair for grief to such a degree that <hi type="italic">on all their heads shall be baldness, and they shall cut off their beards,</hi> according to the customary expressions of mourning in those times and countries. When they go abroad they shall be so far from coveting to appear handsome that <hi type="italic">in the streets they shall gird themselves with sackcloth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.3">v. 3</reference>), and perhaps being forced to use that poor clothing, the enemy having stripped them, and rifled their houses, and left them no other clothing. When they come home, instead of applying themselves to their business, they shall go up to <hi type="italic">the tops of their houses</hi> which were flat-roofed, and there they shall <hi type="italic">weep abundantly,</hi> nay, they shall <hi type="italic">howl,</hi> in crying to their gods. Those that <hi type="italic">cry not to God with their hearts</hi> do but <hi type="italic">howl upon their beds,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.7.14">Hos. vii. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.3">Amos viii. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">They shall come down with weeping</hi> (so the margin reads it); they shall come down from their high places and the tops of their houses weeping as much as they did when they went up. Prayer to the true God is heart's ease (<reference osisRef="1Sam.1.18">1 Sam. i. 18</reference>), but prayers to false gods are not. Divers places are here named that should be full of lamentation (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.4">v. 4</reference>), and it is but a poor relief to have so many fellow-sufferers, fellow-mourners; to a public spirit it is rather an aggravation <hi type="italic">socios habuisse doloris—to have associates in woe.</hi> <div eID="gen15826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15827" type="x-p"/> IV. That the courage of their militia should fail them. Though they were bred soldiers, and were well armed, yet they <hi type="italic">shall cry out</hi> and shriek for fear, and every one of them shall have <hi type="italic">his life become grievous to him,</hi> though it is characteristic of a military life to delight in danger, <reference osisRef="Isa.15.4">v. 4</reference>. See how easily God can dispirit the stoutest of men, and deprive a nation of benefit by those whom it most depended upon for strength and defence. The Moabites shall generally be so overwhelmed with grief that life itself shall be a burden to them. God can easily make weary of life those that are fondest of it. <div eID="gen15827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15828" type="x-p"/> V. That the outcry for these calamities should propagate grief to all the adjacent parts, <reference osisRef="Isa.15.5">v. 5</reference>. 1. The prophet himself has very sensible impressions made upon his spirit by the prediction of it: "<hi type="italic">My heart shall cry out for Moab;</hi> though they are enemies to Israel, they are our fellow-creatures, of the same rank with us, and therefore it should grieve us to see them in such distress, the rather because we know not how soon it may be our own turn to drink of the same cup of trembling." Note, It becomes God's ministers to be of a tender spirit, not to desire the woeful day, but to be like their master, who wept over Jerusalem even when he gave her up to ruin, like their God, <hi type="italic">who desires not the death of sinners.</hi> 2. All the neighbouring cities shall echo to the lamentations of Moab. <hi type="italic">The fugitives,</hi> who are making the best of their way to shift for their own safety, shall carry the cry to <hi type="italic">Zoar,</hi> the city to which their ancestor Lot fled for shelter from Sodom's flames and which was spared for his sake. They shall make as great a noise with their cry <hi type="italic">as a heifer of three years old</hi> does when she goes <hi type="italic">lowing</hi> for her calf, as <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.12">1 Sam. vi. 12</reference>. They shall go up the hill of <hi type="italic">Luhith</hi> (as David went up the ascent of Mount Olivet, many a weary step and all in tears, <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2 Sam. xv. 30</reference>), and <hi type="italic">in the way of Horonaim</hi> (a dual termination), the way that leads to the two Beth-horons, the upper and the nether, which we read of, <reference osisRef="Josh.16.3">Josh. xvi. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.16.5">5</reference>. Thither the cry shall be carried, there it shall be raised, even at that great distance: <hi type="italic">A cry of destruction;</hi> that shall be the cry, like, "Fire, fire! we are all undone." Grief is catching, so is fear, and justly, for trouble is spreading and when it begins who knows where it will end?
entries.6ce8c5b7d9d5bae5d274a9f4975958d49e6a9acd: <div eID="gen15828" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Burden of Moab. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 725.)</title> <div sID="gen15829" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> For the waters of Nimrim shall be desolate: for the hay is withered away, the grass faileth, there is no green thing. <hi type="super">7</hi> Therefore the abundance they have gotten, and that which they have laid up, shall they carry away to the brook of the willows. <hi type="super">8</hi> For the cry is gone round about the borders of Moab; the howling thereof unto Eglaim, and the howling thereof unto Beer-elim. <hi type="super">9</hi> For the waters of Dimon shall be full of blood: for I will bring more upon Dimon, lions upon him that escapeth of Moab, and upon the remnant of the land. <div eID="gen15829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15830" type="x-p"/> Here the prophet further describes the woeful and piteous lamentations that should be heard throughout all the country of Moab when it should become a prey to the Assyrian army. "By this time <hi type="italic">the cry has gone round about</hi> all <hi type="italic">the borders of Moab,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.15.8">v. 8</reference>. Every corner of the country has received the alarm, and is in the utmost confusion upon it. It has reached to <hi type="italic">Eglaim,</hi> a city at one end of the country, and to <hi type="italic">Beer-elim,</hi> a city as far the other way. Where sin has been general, and all flesh have corrupted their way, what can be expected but a general desolation? Two things are here spoken of as causes of this lamentation:— <div eID="gen15830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15831" type="x-p"/> I. <hi type="italic">The waters of Nimrim are desolate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.6">v. 6</reference>), that is, the country is plundered and impoverished, and all the wealth and substance of it swept away by the victorious army. Famine is usually the sad effect of war. Look into the fields that were well watered, the fruitful meadows that yielded delightful prospects and more delightful products, and there all is eaten up, or carried off by the enemy's foragers, and the remainder trodden to dirt by their horses. If an army encamp upon green fields, their greenness is soon gone. Look into the houses, and they are stripped too (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">The abundance</hi> of wealth that <hi type="italic">they had gotten</hi> with a great deal of art and industry, and <hi type="italic">that which they had laid up</hi> with a great deal of care and confidence, <hi type="italic">shall they carry away to the brook of the willows.</hi> Either the owners shall carry it thither to hide it or the enemies shall carry it thither to pack it up and send it home, by water perhaps, to their own country. Note, 1. Those that are eager to get abundance of this world, and solicitous to lay up what they have gotten, little consider what may become of it and in how short a time it may be all taken from them. Great abundance, by tempting the robbers, exposes the owners; and those who depend upon it to protect them often find it does but betray them. 2. In times of distress great riches are often great burdens, and do but increase the owner's care or the enemies' strength. <hi type="italic">Cantabit vacuus coram latrone viator—The penniless traveller will exult, when accosted by a robber, in having nothing about him.</hi> <div eID="gen15831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15832" type="x-p"/> II. <hi type="italic">The waters of Dimon are turned into blood</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.9">v. 9</reference>), that is, the inhabitants of the country are slain in great numbers, so that the waters adjoining to the cities, whether rivers or pools, are discoloured with human gore, inhumanly shed like water. <hi type="italic">Dimon</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">bloody;</hi> the place shall answer to its name. Perhaps it was that place in the country of Moab where the waters seemed to the <hi type="italic">Moabites as blood</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.22-2Kgs.3.23">2 Kings iii. 22, 23</reference>), which occasioned their overthrow. But now, says God, <hi type="italic">I will bring more upon Dimon,</hi> more blood than was shed, or thought to be seen, at that time. <hi type="italic">I will bring additions upon Dimon</hi> (so the word is), additional plagues; I have yet more judgments in reserve for them. <hi type="italic">For all this, God's anger is not turned away.</hi> When he judges he will overcome; and to the roll of curses shall be <hi type="italic">added many like words,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.36.32">Jer. xxxvi. 32</reference>. See here what is the <hi type="italic">yet more evil</hi> to be brought upon Dimon, upon Moab, which is now to be made a land of blood. Some flee, and make their escape, others sit still, and are overlooked, and are as a remnant of the land; but upon both God <hi type="italic">will bring lions,</hi> beasts of prey (which are reckoned one of God's four judgments, <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.21">Ezek. xiv. 21</reference>), and these shall glean up those that have escaped the sword of the enemy. Those that continue impenitent in sin, when they are preserved from one judgment, are but reserved for another.  <chapter eID="Isa.15"/> <div eID="gen15832" type="x-p"/>

entries.0197a642cecc9dd1279f44958434fdc27ee1753f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8602"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 15</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.15.1-Isa.15.9">Is 15:1-9</reference>. The Fifteenth and Sixteenth Chapters Form One Prophecy on Moab.</title> <div sID="gen14096" type="x-p"/> Lowth thinks it was delivered in the first years of Hezekiah's reign and fulfilled in the fourth when Shalmaneser, on his way to invade Israel, may have seized on the strongholds of Moab. Moab probably had made common cause with Israel and Syria in a league against Assyria. Hence it incurred the vengeance of Assyria. Jeremiah has introduced much of this prophecy into his forty-eighth chapter.<div eID="gen14096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14097" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8602"/><hi type="bold">1. Because--</hi>rather, "Surely"; literally, "(I affirm) that" [Maurer].<div eID="gen14097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14098" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">night--</hi>the time best suited for a hostile incursion (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.4">Is 21:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.39.4">Jr 39:4</reference>).<div eID="gen14098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14099" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ar--</hi>meaning in Hebrew, "the city"; the metropolis of Moab, on the south of the river Arnon.<div eID="gen14099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Kir--</hi>literally, "a citadel"; not far from Ar, towards the south.<div eID="gen14100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14101" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">He--</hi>Moab personified.<div eID="gen14101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bajith--</hi>rather, "to the temple" [Maurer]; answering to the "sanctuary" (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.12">Is 16:12</reference>), in a similar context.<div eID="gen14102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to Dibon--</hi>Rather, as Dibon was in a plain north of the Arnon, "Dibon (is gone up) to the high places," the usual places of sacrifice in the East. Same town as Dimon (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.9">Is 15:9</reference>).<div eID="gen14103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to weep--</hi>at the sudden calamity.<div eID="gen14104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14105" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">over Nebo--</hi>rather "in Nebo"; not "on account of" Nebo (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.15.3">Is 15:3</reference>) [Maurer]. The town Nebo was adjacent to the mountain, not far from the northern shore of the Dead Sea. There it was that Chemosh, the idol of Moab, was worshipped (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.34.1">De 34:1</reference>).<div eID="gen14105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Medeba--</hi>south of Heshbon, on a hill east of Jordan.<div eID="gen14106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14107" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">baldness ... beard cut off--</hi>The Orientals regarded the beard with peculiar veneration. To cut one's beard off is the greatest mark of sorrow and mortification (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.48.37">Jr 48:37</reference>). <div eID="gen14107" type="x-p"/>
entries.e984991334945d222b7bee9ad7e37b11bea8ecb6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8603"/><div sID="gen14108" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8603"/><hi type="bold">3. tops of ... houses--</hi>flat; places of resort for prayer, &c., in the East (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.9">Ac 10:9</reference>).<div eID="gen14108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weeping abundantly--</hi>"melting away in tears." Horsley prefers "descending to weep." Thus there is a "parallelism by alternate construction" [Lowth], or chiasmus; "howl" refers to "tops of houses." "Descending to weep" to "streets" or squares, whither they descend from the housetops. <div eID="gen14109" type="x-p"/>
entries.a426c8261f705203697787f0bec7e04fb8cb33e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8604"/><div sID="gen14110" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8604"/><hi type="bold">4. Heshbon--</hi>an Amorite city, twenty miles east of Jordan; taken by Moab after the carrying away of Israel (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.48.1-Jer.48.47">Jr 48:1-47</reference>).<div eID="gen14110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14111" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Elealeh--</hi>near Heshbon, in Reuben.<div eID="gen14111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14112" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jahaz--</hi>east of Jordan, in Reuben. Near it Moses defeated Sihon.<div eID="gen14112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14113" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">therefore--</hi>because of the sudden overthrow of their cities. Even the armed men, instead of fighting in defense of their land, shall join in the general cry.<div eID="gen14113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14114" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">life, &c.--</hi>rather, "his soul is grieved" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.1.8">1Sa 1:8</reference>) [Maurer]. <div eID="gen14114" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4ae92395636aa5675029aacb3314c5cb67e73fc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8605"/><div sID="gen14115" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8605"/><hi type="bold">5. My--</hi>The prophet himself is moved with pity for Moab. Ministers, in denouncing the wrath of God against sinners, should do it with tender sorrow, not with exultation.<div eID="gen14115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14116" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fugitives--</hi>fleeing from Moab, wander as far as to Zoar, on the extreme boundary south of the Dead Sea. Horsley translates, "her nobility," or "rulers" (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.18">Ho 4:18</reference>).<div eID="gen14116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14117" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heifer, &c.--</hi>that is, raising their voices "like a heifer" (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.48.34">Jr 48:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.36">36</reference>). The expression "three years old," implies one at its full vigor (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.9">Ge 15:9</reference>), as yet not brought under the yoke; as Moab heretofore unsubdued, but now about to be broken. So <reference osisRef="Jer.31.18">Jr 31:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.4.13">Ho 4:13</reference>. Maurer translates, "Eglath" (in English Version, "a heifer") Shelishijah (that is, the third, to distinguish it from two others of the same name).<div eID="gen14117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14118" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the mounting up--</hi>up the ascent.<div eID="gen14118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14119" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Luhith--</hi>a mountain in Moab.<div eID="gen14119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14120" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Horonaim--</hi>a town of Moab not far from Zoar (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.5">Jr 48:5</reference>). It means "the two poles," being near caves.<div eID="gen14120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14121" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cry of destruction--</hi>a cry appropriate to the destruction which visits their country. <div eID="gen14121" type="x-p"/>
entries.1eeaa4e2bf108bb42bf74becb0b6fb6d3762f64f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8606"/><div sID="gen14122" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8606"/><hi type="bold">6. For--</hi>the cause of their flight southwards (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.19">2Ki 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.25">25</reference>). "For" the northern regions and even the city Nimrim (the very name of which means "limpid waters," in Gilead near Jordan) are without water or herbage. <div eID="gen14122" type="x-p"/>
entries.4e0d185c219ebefcdd5fd060cfd650e982679bc8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8607"/><div sID="gen14123" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8607"/><hi type="bold">7. Therefore--</hi>because of the devastation of the land.<div eID="gen14123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abundance--</hi>literally, "that which is over and above" the necessaries of life.<div eID="gen14124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14125" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brook of ... willows--</hi>The fugitives flee from Nimrim, where the waters have failed, to places better watered. Margin has "valley of Arabians"; that is, to the valley on the boundary between them and Arabia-Petræa; now Wady-el Arabah. "Arabia" means a "desert." <div eID="gen14125" type="x-p"/>
entries.2764d21c4234161d4f2ed8508ac577b463d18ef8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8608"/><div sID="gen14126" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8608"/><hi type="bold">8. Eglaim--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.10">Eze 47:10</reference>), En-eglaim. Not the Agalum of Eusebius, eight miles from Areopolis towards the south; the context requires a town on the very borders of Moab or beyond them.<div eID="gen14126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Beer-elim--</hi>literally, "the well of the Princes"--(so <reference osisRef="Num.21.16-Num.21.18">Nu 21:16-18</reference>). Beyond the east borders of Moab. <div eID="gen14127" type="x-p"/>
entries.3035f16fa5839c101f8a6b9fb9d992c281a8fd27: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8609"/><div sID="gen14128" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8609"/><hi type="bold">9. Dimon--</hi>same as Dibon (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.2">Is 15:2</reference>). Its waters are the Arnon.<div eID="gen14128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14129" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">full of blood--</hi>The slain of Moab shall be so many.<div eID="gen14129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14130" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring more--</hi>fresh calamities, namely, the "lions" afterwards mentioned (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.25">2Ki 17:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.6">Jr 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.15.3">15:3</reference>). Vitringa understands Nebuchadnezzar as meant by "the lion"; but it is plural, "lions." The "more," or in Hebrew, "additions," he explains of the addition made to the waters of Dimon by the streams of blood of the slain. <chapter eID="Isa.15"/>

entries.82b8f5c1158a9f84b0531ec5b09d413bc3471f97: <div eID="gen27149" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27150" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27151" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27151" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27150" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27152" type="x-p"/> Prediction of very heavy calamities about to fall upon the Moabites, <reference osisRef="Isa.15.1-Isa.15.9">Isa 15:1-9</reference>. <div eID="gen27152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27153" type="x-p"/> This and the following chapter, taken together, make one entire prophecy, very improperly divided into two parts. The time of its delivery, and consequently of its accomplishment, which was to be in three years from that time, is uncertain; the former not being marked in the prophecy itself, nor the latter recorded in history. But the most probable account is, that it was delivered soon after the foregoing, in the first year of Hezekiah; and that it was accomplished in his fourth year, when Shalmaneser invaded the kingdom of Israel. He might probably march through Moab; and to secure every thing behind him, possess himself of the whole country, by taking their principal strong places Ar and Kirhares. - L. The authorized Version which we have followed in the margin, places the prophecy in this chapter fourteen years earlier than that contained in the two preceding. <div eID="gen27153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27154" type="x-p"/> Jeremiah has happily introduced much of this prophecy of Isaiah into his own larger prophecy against the same people in his forty-eighth chapter, denouncing God's judgment on Moab, subsequent to the calamity here foretold, and to be executed by Nebuchadnezzar; by which means several mistakes of transcribers in the present text of both prophets may be rectified. <div eID="gen27154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27155" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27156" type="x-p"/> Because in the night - בליל beleil. That both these cities should be taken in the night is a circumstance somewhat unusual; but not so material as to deserve to be so strongly insisted upon. Vitringa, by his remark on this word, shows that he was dissatisfied with it in its plain and obvious meaning, and is forced to have recourse to a very hard metaphorical interpretation of it. Noctu vel nocturno impetu; vel metaphorice, repente, subito, inexpectata destructione: placet posterius. Calmet conjectures, and I think it probable, that the true reading is כליל keleil, as the night. There are many mistakes in the Hebrew text arising from the very great similitude of the letters ב beth, and כ caph, which in many MSS., and some printed editions, are hardly distinguishable. <div eID="gen27156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27157" type="x-p"/> Admitting this reading, the translation will be, - "Because Ar is utterly destroyed, Moab is undone! <div eID="gen27157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27158" type="x-p"/> Because Kir is utterly destroyed, Moab is undone!"
entries.480d776e9e7f264c23965988f0ae1dd74ec1fdeb: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen27158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27159" type="x-p"/> He is gone to Bajith, and to Dibon - עלה הבית alah habbayith, should be rendered, he is gone to the House, i.e., to their chief temple, where they practiced idolatry. Dibon was the name of a tower where also was an idolatrous temple; thither they went to weep and pray before their idols, that they might interpose and save them from their calamities. So R. D. Kimchi. Me is gone to Bajith and to Dibon: but Bishop Lowth reads Beth Dibon; this is the name of one place; and the two words are to be joined together, without the ו vau intervening. So the Chaldee and Syriac. This reading is not supported by any MS. or Version: but some MSS., instead of ער ar, have עיר ir, a city, others have עד ad, unto, and some editions have על al, upon. But all these help little, though they show that the place puzzled both the scribes and the editors. <div eID="gen27159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27160" type="x-p"/> On all their heads shall be baldness, etc." On every head there is baldness," etc. - Herodotus, 2:36, speaks of it as a general practice among all men, except the Egyptians, to cut off their hair as a token of mourning. "Cut off thy hair, and cast it away," says Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.29">Jer 7:29</reference>, "and take up a lamentation." Τουτο νυ και γερας οιον οἱζυροισι βροτοισι Κειρασθαι τε κομην, βαλεειν τ' απο δακρυ παρειων. <div eID="gen27160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27161" type="x-p"/> Hom. Odyss. 4:197. "The rites of wo <div eID="gen27161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27162" type="x-p"/> Are all, alas! the living can bestow; <div eID="gen27162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27163" type="x-p"/> O'er the congenial dust enjoined to shear <div eID="gen27163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27164" type="x-p"/> The graceful curl, and drop the tender tear." <div eID="gen27164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27165" type="x-p"/> Pope. <div eID="gen27165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27166" type="x-p"/> On every head. - For ראשיו roshaiv, read ראש rosh. So the parallel place, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.37">Jer 48:37</reference>, and so three MSS., one ancient. An ancient MS. reads על כל ראש al col rosh. Five read בכל ראש bechol rosh, on every head, with the Septuagint and Arabic. And every head. The ו vau, and, is found in thirty MSS., in three editions, and in the Syriac, Vulgate, and Chaldee. <div eID="gen27166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27167" type="x-p"/> Cut off "Shorn" - The printed editions, as well as the MSS., are divided on the reading of this word. Some have גדועה geduah, shorn, others גרעה geruah, diminished. The similitude of the letters ד daleth and ר resh has likewise occasioned many mistakes. In the present case, the sense is pretty much the same with either reading. The text of <reference osisRef="Jer.48.37">Jer 48:37</reference> has the latter, diminished. The former reading is found in twelve of Dr. Zennicott's MSS., forty of De Rossi's, and two of my own. A great number of editions have the same reading.
entries.485cdb7efe3ec09ab0a3e39494c93304ab31f6e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen27167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27168" type="x-p"/> With sackcloth - שק sak. The word is in the plural שקים sakkim, sacks, in one of De Rossi's MSS.
entries.8d8fe5c28d17ffbae99ad7691ad981a9258cda53: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen27168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27169" type="x-p"/> The armed soldiers "The very loins" - So the Septuagint, ἡ οσφυς, and the Syriac. They cry out violently, with their utmost force.
entries.b0758739cd05d5939efb49c9f54b87fbba4e1787: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27170" type="x-p"/> My heart shall cry out for Moab "The heart of Moab crieth within her" - For לבי libbi, my heart, the Septuagint reads לבו libbo, his heart, or לב leb; the Chaldee, לבו libbo. For בריחיה bericheyha, the Syriac reads ברוחה berocheh; and so likewise the Septuagint, rendering it εν αυτῃ, Edit. Vat: or εν ἑαυτῃ, Edit. Alex. and MSS. I., D. II. <div eID="gen27170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27171" type="x-p"/> A heifer of three years old "A young heifer" - Hebrew, a heifer three years old, in full strength; as Horace uses equa trima, for a young mare just coming to her prime. Bochart observes, from Aristotle, Hist. Animal. lib. 4 that in this kind of animals alone the voice of the female is deeper than that of the male; therefore the lowing of the heifer, rather than of the bullock, is chosen by the prophet, as the more proper image to express the mourning of Moab. But I must add that the expression here is very short and obscure; and the opinions of interpreters are various in regard to the meaning. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.48.34">Jer 48:34</reference>. <div eID="gen27171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27172" type="x-p"/> Shall they go it up "They shall ascend" - For יעלה yaaleh, the Septuagint and a MS. read in the plural, יעלו yaalu. And from this passage the parallel place in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.5">Jer 48:5</reference> must be corrected; where, for יעלה בכי yaaleh bechi, which gives no good sense, read יעלה בו yaaleh bo.
entries.31e7db754c19e1cb420cbce093ee0c0e193faa84: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> "Shall perish" - אבדו abadu or אבדה abadeh. This word seems to have been lost out of the text: it is supplied by the parallel place, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.36">Jer 48:36</reference>. The Syriac expresses it by עבר aber, praeteriit, "he hath passed;" and the Chaldee by יתבזזון yithbazezun, diripientur. <div eID="gen27172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27173" type="x-p"/> To the brook of the willows "To the valley of willows" - That is, to Babylon. Hieron. and Jarchi in loc., both referring to <reference osisRef="Psa.137.2">Psa 137:2</reference>. So likewise Prideaux, Le Clerc, etc.
entries.699a47b5a3587673b66b0af419ad46ed7b9160da: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen27173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27174" type="x-p"/> The waters of Dimon - Some have Dibon, others have Ribon and Rimon. St. Jerome observes that the same town was called both Dibon and Dimon. The reading is therefore indifferent. <div eID="gen27174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27175" type="x-p"/> Upon him that escapeth of Moab, etc. "Upon the escaped of Moab, and Ariel, and the remnant of Admah" - The Septuagint for עריה aryeh, read אריאל ariel. Ar Moab was called also Ariel or Areopolis, Hieron. and Theodoret. See Cellarius. They make אדמה Admah, also a proper name. Michaelis thinks that the Moabites might be called the remnant of Admah, as sprung from Lot and his daughters, escaped from the destruction of that and the other cities; or, metaphorically, as the Jews are called princes of Sodom, and people of Gomorrah, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.10">Isa 1:10</reference>. Bibliotheque Orient. Part v., p. 195. The reading of this verse is very doubtful; and the sense, in every way in which it can be read, very obscure. - L. Calmet thinks there may be a reference to <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.22">1Chr 11:22</reference>, where it is said, "Benaiah slew two lion-like men of Moab," or the two Ariels of Moab, and would therefore translate, "I will bring down the remnant of Moab like Ariel, (which Benaiah smote), and them that are escaped like Adamah." They shall be exterminated, as were the inhabitants of those two cities. Ariel was a double city - the river Arnon dividing it in two. This is the two Ariels of Moab - not two lion-like men, much less two lions. See Calmet on this place.  <chapter eID="Isa.15"/> <div eID="gen27175" type="x-p"/>

entries.b33be81682591963bd46713e068d59e93fb4ea41: <reference osisRef="Isa.15.1">Isa 15:1</reference> <div eID="gen13010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13011" type="x-p"/> There is no other prophecy in the book of Isaiah in which the heart of the prophet is so painfully affected by what his mind sees, and his mouth is obliged to prophesy. All that he predicts evokes his deepest sympathy, just as if he himself belonged to the unfortunate nation to which he is called to be a messenger of woe. He commences with an utterance of amazement. <hi type="italic">“Oracle concerning Moab! for in a night 'Ar-Moab is laid waste, destroyed; for in a night Kir-Moab is laid waste, destroyed.”</hi> The <hi type="italic">ci</hi> (for) is explanatory in both instances, and not simply affirmative, or, as Knobel maintains, recitative, and therefore unmeaning. The prophet justifies the peculiar heading to his prophecy from the horrible vision given him to see, and takes us at once into the very heart of the vision, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1">Isa 17:1</reference>; Isa 23:1. <hi type="italic">'Ar Moab</hi> (in which <hi type="italic">'Ar</hi> is Moabitish for <hi type="italic">'Ir</hi>; cf., <reference osisRef="Jer.49.3">Jer 49:3</reference>, where we find <hi type="italic">'Ai</hi> written instead of <hi type="italic">'Ar</hi>, which we should naturally expect) is the name of the capital of Moab (Grecized, <hi type="italic">Areopolis</hi>), which was situated to the south of the Arnon, at present a large field of ruins, with a village of the name of <hi type="italic">Rabba</hi>. <hi type="italic">Kir Moab</hi> (in which <hi type="italic">Kir</hi> is the Moabitish for <hi type="italic">Kiryah</hi>) was the chief fortress of Joab, which was situated to the south-east of <hi type="italic">Ar</hi>, the present <hi type="italic">Kerek</hi>, where there is still a town with a fortification upon a rock, which can be seen from Jerusalem with a telescope on a clear day, and forms so thoroughly one mass with the rock, that in 1834, when Ibrahim Pasha resolved to pull it down, he was obliged to relinquish the project. The identity of <hi type="italic">Kir</hi> and <hi type="italic">Kerek</hi> is unquestionable, but that of <hi type="italic">Ar</hi> and <hi type="italic">Rabba</hi> has been disputed; and on the ground of Num 22:36, where it seems to be placed nearer the Arnon, it has been transposed to the ruins on the pasture land at the confluence of the <hi type="italic">Lejûm</hi> and <hi type="italic">Mujib</hi> (= “the city that is by the river” in <reference osisRef="Deut.2.36">Deu 2:36</reference> and <reference osisRef="Josh.13.9">Jos 13:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.13.16">Jos 13:16</reference> : see Comm. on Num 21:15) - a conjecture which has this against it, that the name <hi type="italic">Areopolis</hi>, which has been formed from <hi type="italic">Ar</hi>, is attached to the “<hi type="italic">metropolis civitas Ar</hi>,” which was called <hi type="italic">Rabba</hi> as the metropolis, and of which Jerome relates (on the passage before us), as an event associated with his own childhood, that it was then destroyed by an earthquake (probably in 342). The two names of the cities are used as masculine here, like <hi type="italic">Dammesek</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1">Isa 17:1</reference>, and <hi type="italic">Tzor</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.23.1">Isa 23:1</reference>, though it cannot therefore be said, as at Mic 5:1, that the <hi type="italic">city</hi> stands for the <hi type="italic">inhabitants</hi> (Ges. <hi type="italic">Lehrgebäude</hi>, p. 469). “<hi type="italic">In a night</hi>” (ליל absolute, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.21.11">Isa 21:11</reference>, not construct, which would give an illogical assertion, as <hi type="italic">shuddad</hi> and <hi type="italic">nidmâh</hi> are almost coincident, so far as the sense is concerned) the two pillars of the strength of Moab are overthrown. In the space of a night, and therefore very suddenly (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.14">Isa 17:14</reference>), Moab is destroyed. The prophet repeats twice what it would have been quite sufficient to say once, just as if he had been condemned to keep his eye fixed upon the awful spectacle (on the <hi type="italic">asyndeton</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Isa.33.9">Isa 33:9</reference>; and on the <hi type="italic">anadiplosis</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.15.8">Isa 15:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.9">Isa 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.11">Isa 21:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.17.12-Isa.17.13">Isa 17:12-13</reference>). His first sensation is that of horror.
entries.f319fe33c0fcb9f683704cc7ee1fe8b89f64aa2c: <reference osisRef="Isa.15.2-Isa.15.4">Isa 15:2-4</reference> <div eID="gen13011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13012" type="x-p"/> But just as horror, when once it begins to reflect, is dissolved in tears, the thunder-claps in <reference osisRef="Isa.15.1">Isa 15:1</reference> are followed by universal weeping and lamentation. <hi type="italic">“They go up to the temple-house and Dibon, up to the heights to weep: upon Nebo and upon Medebah of Moab there is weeping: on all heads baldness, every beard is mutilated. In the markets of Moab they gird themselves with sackcloth; on the roofs of the land, and in its streets, everything wails, melting into tears. Heshbon cries, and 'Elâle; even to Jahaz they hear their howling; even the armed men of Moab break out into mourning thereat; its soul trembles within it.”</hi> The people (the subject to עלה) ascend the mountain with the temple of <hi type="italic">Chemosh</hi>, the central sanctuary of the land. This temple is called <hi type="italic">hab</hi>-<hi type="italic">baith</hi>, though not that there was a Moabitish town or village with some such name as <hi type="italic">Bêth</hi>-<hi type="italic">Diblathaim</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.22">Jer 48:22</reference>), as Knobel supposes. <hi type="italic">Dibon</hi>, which lay above the Arnon (<hi type="italic">Wady Mujib</hi>), like all the places mentioned in <reference osisRef="Isa.15.2-Isa.15.4">Isa 15:2-4</reference>, at present a heap of ruins, a short hour to the north of the central Arnon, in the splendid plain of <hi type="italic">el-Chura</hi>, had consecrated heights in the neighbourhood (cf., <reference osisRef="Josh.13.17">Jos 13:17</reference>; Num 22:41), and therefore would turn to them. Moab mourns upon <hi type="italic">Nebo</hi> and <hi type="italic">Medebah</hi>; ייליל, for which we find יהיליל in <reference osisRef="Isa.52.5">Isa 52:5</reference>, is written intentionally for a double preformative, instead of ייליל (compare the similar forms in <reference osisRef="Job.24.21">Job 24:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.138.6">Psa 138:6</reference>, and Ges. §70, Anm.). על is to be taken in a local sense, as Hendewerk, Drechsler, and Knobel have rendered it. For Nebo was probably a place situated upon a height on the mountain of that name, towards the south-east of Heshbon (the ruins of <hi type="italic">Nabo</hi>, <hi type="italic">Nabau</hi>, mentioned in the <hi type="italic">Onom</hi>.); and Medebah (still a heap of ruins bearing the same name) stood upon a round hill about two hours to the south-east of Heshbon. According to Jerome, there was an image of Chemosh in Nebo; and among the ruins of Madeba, Seetzen discovered the foundations of a strange temple. There follows here a description of the expressions of pain. Instead of the usual ראשיו, we read ראשיו here. And instead of <hi type="italic">gedu‛âh</hi> (<hi type="italic">abscissae</hi>), Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.37">Jer 48:37</reference>) has, according to his usual style, <hi type="italic">geru'âh</hi> (<hi type="italic">decurtatae</hi>), with the simple alteration of a single letter.<note placement="foot">At the same time, the Masora on this passage before us is for <hi type="italic">geru‛ah</hi> with <hi type="italic">Resh</hi>, and we also find this reading in Nissel, Clodius, Jablonsky, and in earlier editions; whilst Sonc. 1486, Ven. 1521, and others, have <hi type="italic">gedu‛ah</hi>, with <hi type="italic">Daleth</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen13012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13013" type="x-p"/> All runs down with weeping (<hi type="italic">culloh</hi>, written as in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.7">Isa 16:7</reference>; in <reference osisRef="Isa.9.8">Isa 9:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.16">Isa 9:16</reference>, we have <hi type="italic">cullo</hi> instead). In other cases it is the eyes that are said to run down in tears, streams, or water-brooks; but here, by a still bolder metonymy, the whole man is said to flow down to the ground, as if melting in a stream of tears. <hi type="italic">Heshbon</hi> and <hi type="italic">Elale</hi> are still visible in their ruins, which lie only half an hour apart upon their separate hills and are still called by the names <hi type="italic">Husban</hi> and <hi type="italic">el-Al</hi>. They were both situated upon hills which commanded an extensive prospect. And there the cry of woe created an echo which was audible as far as <hi type="italic">Jahaz</hi> (<hi type="italic">Jahza</hi>), the city where the king of Heshbon offered battle to Israel in the time of Moses (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.32">Deu 2:32</reference>). The general mourning was so great, that even the armed men, i.e., the heroes (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.41">Jer 48:41</reference>) of Moab, were seized with despair, and cried out in their anguish (the same figure as in <reference osisRef="Isa.33.7">Isa 33:7</reference>). על־כן(, thereat, namely on account of this universal lamentation. Thus the lamentation was universal, without exception. <hi type="italic">Naphsho</hi> (his soul) refers to Moab as a whole nation. The soul of Moab trembles in all the limbs of the national body; ירעה (forming a play upon the sound with יריעוּ), an Arabic word, and in יריעה a Hebrew word also, signifies <hi type="italic">tremere</hi>, <hi type="italic">huc illuc agitari</hi> - an explanation which we prefer, with Rosenmüller and Gesenius, to the idea that ירע is a secondary verb to רעע, fut. ירע. לו is an ethical dative (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.120.6">Psa 120:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.123.4">Psa 123:4</reference>), throwing the action or the pathos inwardly (see <hi type="italic">Psychology</hi>, p. 152). The heart of the prophet participates in this pain with which Moab is agitated throughout; for, as Rashi observes, it is just in this that the prophets of Israel were distinguished from heathen prophets, such as Balaam for example, viz., that the calamities which they announced to the nations went to their own heart (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.21.3-Isa.21.4">Isa 21:3-4</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Isa.22.4">Isa 22:4</reference>).
entries.4609f7941860624d29385ec6d61ccd356c4a9560: <reference osisRef="Isa.15.5-Isa.15.6">Isa 15:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen13013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13014" type="x-p"/> The difficult words in which the prophet expresses this sympathy we render as follows: <hi type="italic">“My heart, towards Moab it crieth out; its bolts reached to Zoar, the three-year-old heifer.”</hi> The <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> in <hi type="italic">l'Moab</hi> is the same both here and in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.11">Isa 16:11</reference> as in <reference osisRef="Isa.14.8-Isa.14.9">Isa 14:8-9</reference>, viz., “turned toward Moab.” Moab, which was masculine in <reference osisRef="Isa.15.4">Isa 15:4</reference>, is feminine here. We may infer from this that עד־צער בריחה is a statement which concerns Moab as a land. Now, <hi type="italic">berichim</hi> signifies the <hi type="italic">bolts</hi> in every other passage in which it occurs; and it is possible to speak of the bolts of a land with just as much propriety as in <reference osisRef="Lam.2.9">Lam 2:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.51.30">Jer 51:30</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.7">Jon 2:7</reference>) of the bolts of a city. And the statement that the bolts of this land went to <hi type="italic">Zoar</hi> is also a very appropriate one, for Kir Moab and Zoar formed the southern fortified girdle of the land; and Zoar, on the south-western tongue of land which runs into the Dead Sea, was the uttermost fortress of Moab, looking over towards Judah; and in its depressed situation below the level of the sea it formed, as it were, the opposite pole of Kir Moab, the highest point in the high land itself. Hence we agree with Jerome, who adopts the rendering <hi type="italic">vectes ejus usque ad Segor</hi>, whereas all the modern translators have taken the word in the sense of fugitives. <hi type="italic">‛Eglath sheilshiyyâh</hi>, which Rosenmüller, Knobel, Drechsler, Meier, and others have taken quite unnecessarily as a proper name, is either in apposition to Zoar or to Moab. In the former case it is a distinguishing epithet. An ox of the three years, or more literally of the third year (cf., <hi type="italic">meshullesheth</hi>, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.9">Gen 15:9</reference>), i.e., a three-year-old ox, is one that is still in all the freshness and fulness of its strength, and that has not yet been exhausted by the length of time that it has worn the yoke. The application of the term to the Moabitish nation is favoured by <reference osisRef="Jer.46.20">Jer 46:20</reference>, where Egypt is called “a very fair heifer” (<hi type="italic">‛eglâh</hi> <hi type="italic">yephēh</hi>-<hi type="italic">phiyyâh</hi>), whilst Babylon is called the same in <reference osisRef="Jer.50.11">Jer 50:11</reference> (cf., Hos 4:16; Hos 10:11). And in the same way, according to the lxx, Vulg., Targum, and Gesenius, Moab is called <hi type="italic">juvenca tertii anni, h. e. indomita jugoque non assueta</hi>, as a nation that was still in the vigour of youth, and if it had hitherto borne the yoke, had always shaken it off again. But the application of it to Zoar is favoured (1.) by <reference osisRef="Jer.48.34">Jer 48:34</reference>, where this epithet is applied to another Moabitish city; (2.) by the accentuation; and (3.) by the fact that in the other case we should expect <hi type="italic">berı̄châh</hi> (the three-year-old heifer, i.e., Moab, is a fugitive to Zoar: vid., Luzzatto). Thus Zoar, the fine, strong, and hitherto unconquered city, is now the destination of the wildest flight before the foe that is coming from the north. A blow has fallen upon Joab, that is more terrible than any that has preceded it. <div eID="gen13014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13015" type="x-p"/> In a few co-ordinate clauses the prophet now sets before us the several scenes of mourning and desolation. <hi type="italic">“for the mountain slope of Luhith they ascend with weeping; for on the road to Horonayim they lift up a cry of despair. For the waters of Nimrim are waste places from this time forth: for the grass is dried up, the vegetation wasteth away, the green is gone.”</hi> The road to <hi type="italic">Luhith</hi> (according to the <hi type="italic">Onom</hi>. between Ar-Moab and Zoar, and therefore in the centre of Moabitis proper) led up a height, and the road to <hi type="italic">Horonayim</hi> (according to <reference osisRef="Jer.48.5">Jer 48:5</reference>) down a slope. Weeping, they ran up to the mountain city to hide themselves there (<hi type="italic">bo</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.24.3">Psa 24:3</reference>; in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.5">Jer 48:5</reference> it is written incorrectly בּכי). Raising loud cries of despair, they stand in front of Horonayim, which lay below, and was more exposed to the enemy. יעערוּ is softened from יערערוּ (possibly to increase the resemblance to an echo), like כּוכב from כּבכּב. The Septuagint renders it very well, κραυγὴν συντριμμοῦ ἐξαναγεροῦσιν - an unaccustomed expression of intense and ever renewed cries at the threatening danger of utter destruction, and with the hope of procuring relief and assistance (<hi type="italic">sheber</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.28">Isa 1:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.26">Isa 30:26</reference>). From the farthest south the scene would suddenly be transferred to the extreme north of the territory of Moab, if <hi type="italic">Nimrim</hi> were the <hi type="italic">Nimra</hi> (<hi type="italic">Beth-Nimra</hi>, Talm. <hi type="italic">nimrin</hi>) which was situated near to the Jordan in Gilead, and therefore farther north than any of the places previously mentioned, and the ruins of which lie a little to the south of Salt, and are still called <hi type="italic">Nimrin</hi>. But the name itself, which is derived from the vicinity of fresh water (Arab. <hi type="italic">nemir</hi>, <hi type="italic">nemı̄r</hi>, clear, pure, sound), is one of frequent occurrence; and even to the south of Moabitis proper there is a <hi type="italic">Wadi Numere</hi>, and a brook called <hi type="italic">Moyet Numere</hi> (two diminutives: “dear little stream of Nimra”), which flows through stony tracks, and which formerly watered the country (Burckhardt, Seetzen, and De Saulcy). In all probability the ruins of <hi type="italic">Numere</hi> by the side of this wady are the Nimrim referred to here, and the waters of the brook the “waters of Nimrim” (<hi type="italic">me Nimrim</hi>). The waters that flowed fresh from the spring had been filled up with rubbish by the enemy, and would now probably lie waste for ever (a similar expression to that in <reference osisRef="Isa.17.2">Isa 17:2</reference>). He had gone through the land scorching and burning, so that all the vegetation had vanished. On the miniature-like short sentences, see <reference osisRef="Isa.29.20">Isa 29:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.8-Isa.33.9">Isa 33:8-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.10">Isa 32:10</reference>; and on היה לא (“it is not in existence,” or “it has become not,” i.e., annihilated), vid., Eze 21:32.
entries.100d93bd563077961e5bf858d3dc3f7005530f74: <reference osisRef="Isa.15.7-Isa.15.9">Isa 15:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen13015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13016" type="x-p"/> As Moabitis has thus become a great scene of conflagration, the Moabites cross the border and fly to Idumaea. The reason for this is given in sentences which the prophet again links on to one another with the particle ci (for). <hi type="italic">“Therefore what has been spared, what has been gained, and their provision, they carry it over the willow-brook. For the scream has gone the round in the territory of Moab; the wailing of Joab resounds to Eglayim, and his wailing to Beeer-Elim. For the waters of Dimon are full of blood: for I suspend over Dimon a new calamity, over the escaped of Moab a lion, and over the remnant of the land.”</hi> <hi type="italic">Yithrâh</hi> is what is superfluous or exceeds the present need, and <hi type="italic">pekuddâh</hi> (lit. a laying up, <hi type="italic">depositio</hi>) that which has been carefully stored; whilst <hi type="italic">‛âsâh</hi>, as the derivative passage, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.36">Jer 48:36</reference>, clearly shows (although the accusative in the whole of <reference osisRef="Isa.15.7">Isa 15:7</reference> is founded upon a different view: see Rashi), is an attributive clause (what has been made, worked out, or gained). All these things they carry across <hi type="italic">nachal hâ‛arâbim</hi>, i.e., not the desert-stream, as Hitzig, Maurer, Ewald, and Knobel suppose, since the plural of <hi type="italic">‛arâbâh</hi> is <hi type="italic">‛arâboth</hi>, but either the Arab stream (lxx, <hi type="italic">Saad</hi>.), or the willow-stream, <hi type="italic">torrens salicum</hi> (Vulg.). The latter is more suitable to the connection; and among the rivers which flow to the south of the Arnon from the mountains of the Moabitish highlands down to the Dead Sea, there is one which is called <hi type="italic">Wadi Sufsaf</hi>, i.e., willow-brook (<hi type="italic">Tzaphtzâphâh</hi> is the name of a brook in Hebrew also), viz., the northern arm of the <hi type="italic">Seil</hi> <hi type="italic">el</hi>-<hi type="italic">Kerek</hi>. This is what we suppose to be intended here, and not the <hi type="italic">Wadi</hi> <hi type="italic">el</hi>-<hi type="italic">Ahsa</hi>, although the latter (probably the biblical <hi type="italic">Zered</hi><note placement="foot">Hence the Targ. II renders <hi type="italic">nachal zered</hi> “the brook of the willows.” See Buxtorf, <hi type="italic">Lex. chald. s.v. Zerad</hi>.)</note> is the boundary river on the extreme south, and separates Moab from Edom (<hi type="italic">Kerek</hi> from <hi type="italic">Gebal</hi>: see Ritter, Erdk. xv 1223-4). Wading through the willow-brook, they carry their possessions across, and hurry off to the land of Edom, for their own land has become the prey of the foe throughout its whole extent, and within its boundaries the cry of wailing passes from <hi type="italic">Eglayim</hi>, on the south-west of Ar, and therefore not far from the southern extremity of the Dead Sea (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.10">Eze 47:10</reference>), as far as <hi type="italic">Beer-elim</hi>, in the north-east of the land towards the desert (Num 21:16-18; עד must be supplied: Ewald, §351, <hi type="italic">a</hi>), that is to say, if we draw a diagonal through the land, from one end to the other. Even the waters of <hi type="italic">Dibon</hi>, which are called <hi type="italic">Dimon</hi> here to produce a greater resemblance in sound to <hi type="italic">dâm</hi>, blood, and by which we are probably to understand the <hi type="italic">Arnon</hi>, as this was only a short distance off (just as in Jdg 5:19 the “waters of Megiddo” are the <hi type="italic">Kishon</hi>), are full of blood,<note placement="foot">דם מלאוּ, with <hi type="italic">munach</hi> (which also represents the metheg) at the first syllable of the verb (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.15.4">Isa 15:4</reference>, לּו ירעה, with <hi type="italic">mercha</hi>), according to Vened. 1521, and other good editions. This is also grammatically correct.</note> so that the enemy must have penetrated into the very heart of the land in his course of devastation and slaughter. But what drives them across the willow-brook is not this alone; it is as if they forebode that what has hitherto occurred is not the worst or the last. Jehovah suspends (<hi type="italic">shith</hi>, as in Hos 6:11) over Dibon, whose waters are already reddened with blood, <hi type="italic">nōsâphōth</hi>, something to be added, i.e., a still further judgment, namely <hi type="italic">a lion</hi>. The measure of Moab’s misfortunes is not yet full: after the northern enemy, a lion will come upon those that have escaped by flight or have been spared at home (on the expression itself, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.10.20">Isa 10:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.32">Isa 37:32</reference>, and other passages). This lion is no other than the basilisk of the prophecy against Philistia, but with this difference, that the basilisk represents one particular Davidic king, whilst the lion is Judah generally, whose emblem was the lion from the time of Jacob’s blessing, in Gen 49:9.  <chapter eID="Isa.15"/> <div eID="gen13016" type="x-p"/>

entries.6814f56cabea7325b9070dc76d8378b220ab251f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.15.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.15.1" sID="gen42769" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42770" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">The burden of Moab.</hi> Here the Prophet prophesies against the <hi type="italic">Moabites</hi>, who were neighbors to the Jews and related to them by blood; for we know that the <hi type="italic">Moabites</hi> were descended from Lot, who was Abraham’s nephew. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.11.31 Bible:Gen.19.37">Genesis 11:31, 19:37</reference>.) Those nations being so closely related, humanity at least demanded that they should maintain some friendly intercourse with each other. But no relationship prevented the <hi type="italic">Moabites</hi> from cherishing hostility towards the Jews, or even from harassing them whenever it was in their power; which is an evidence of a savage and barbarous disposition. To them also, on account of their cruelty towards the people of God, to whom they ought to have conducted themselves with brotherly love, the Prophet therefore threatens destruction.<div eID="gen42770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42771" type="x-p"/>We ought to remember the design of these predictions. It cannot be believed that they were of any advantage to the <hi type="italic">Moabites</hi>, even though they had heard from the mouth of the Prophet himself the words which we read; but he neither addressed them with his voice, nor sent to them a written communication. It was therefore to believers, rather than to them, that the Prophet looked, and for two reasons. The first reason was, that when they saw so many changes taking place, cities overturned, kingdoms destroyed and succeeding one another, they might not think that this world is governed by the blind violence of fortune, but might acknowledge the providence of God. If nothing had been foretold, the minds of men, having a strong tendency to foolishness, and being strangely blind to the works of God, might have been disposed to attribute all this to chance; but when they had been forewarned by the Prophets, they beheld the judgments of God as from a lofty watch-tower. To us also in the present day Isaiah has, as it were, pointed out with the finger what was then hidden. In his predictions we behold God sitting on his judgment-seat, and regulating everything according to his pleasure; and although the wicked in various ways vented their mad rage, still the Lord made use of their agency to execute his judgments. The second design which the prophets had in view was, that while the whole world was shaken, the Jews might know that God took care of their safety, and that he testified the warmth of his affection for the Church, by taking vengeance on her enemies by whom she had been barbarously treated.<div eID="gen42771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42772" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Ar-Moab.</hi> The Hebrew word <foreign xml:lang="he">ער</foreign> (<hi type="italic">Ar</hi>) means <hi type="italic">a city</hi>; as <foreign xml:lang="he">קיר</foreign> (<hi type="italic">kir</hi>) means <hi type="italic">a wall</hi>; but as <foreign xml:lang="he">ער מואב</foreign> (<hi type="italic">Ar-Moab</hi>) was one of the chief cities of the <hi type="italic">Moabites</hi>, it is supposed to be here a proper name. We might indeed explain both words as appellatives, to convey a threatening of the overthrow of the fortified towns of which the <hi type="italic">Moabites</hi> are proud; but I rather adopt the ordinary interpretation. Here therefore Isaiah has given a description, that we may behold in it the overthrow of the Moabites, when their chief cities are destroyed.<div eID="gen42772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42773" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">In the night.</hi> By <hi type="italic">the night</hi> he means a sudden and unexpected occurrence, which the Moabites did not dread. <hi type="italic">Night</hi> being appropriated to rest, if anything happen at that time, it is viewed as sudden and unlooked for, and therefore excites violent alarm. Besides, he intended to rebuke the Moabites for being free from anxiety, considering themselves to be fortified by defences on every hand, and placed beyond the reach of all danger.<div eID="gen42773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42774" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Is brought to silence.</hi> That is, <hi type="italic">is destroyed</hi>, and hence also <hi type="italic">Silence</hi> sometimes means Death. Others disregard the metaphor, and choose to render it, <hi type="italic">She is cut off</hi>; but I leave that point undecided. What Isaiah declares as to the <hi type="italic">Moabites</hi>, Scripture pronounces as to the reprobate, that destruction is at hand, and, when they are looking for nothing of that kind, will fearfully overwhelm them. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.23.19 Bible:1Thess.5.2 Bible:1Thess.5.3">Jeremiah 23:19; 1 Thessalonians 5:2, 3</reference>.)<div eID="gen42774" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.15.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42769" osisID="Isa.15.1" type="section"/>
entries.31b83313c336e52c0d93bbba88e940af04663689: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.15.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.15.2" sID="gen42775" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42776" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> <hi type="italic">He shall go up into the house.</hi> <note n="236"> <div sID="gen42777" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">He is gone up to Bajith</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42778" type="x-p"/> FT228 <hi type="italic">He is gone up to Moab into the house</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Jarchi</hi>. Breithaupt remarks that the Hebrew word <foreign xml:lang="he">הבית</foreign> (<hi type="italic">habbaith</hi>) is sometimes viewed as a proper name, and that in the version of Junius and Tremellius it is rendered <hi type="italic">Bajith</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen42778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42779" type="x-p"/> FT229 “Shaving the head and face are the eastern tokens of mourning for the dead. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.24">Isaiah 3:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.41.5">Jeremiah 41:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Mic.1.16">Micah 1:16</reference>.)” — <hi type="italic">Rosenmuller</hi><div eID="gen42779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42780" type="x-p"/> FT230 <hi type="italic">In their streets</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42781" type="x-p"/> FT231 <hi type="italic">Weeping abundantly</hi>. (Heb. <hi type="italic">descending into weeping</hi>, or, <hi type="italic">coming down with weeping</hi>.) — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42782" type="x-p"/> FT232 <hi type="italic">His life shall be grievous unto him</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42783" type="x-p"/> FT233 <hi type="italic">His fugitives</hi> shall flee<hi type="italic"> unto Zoar, an heifer of three</hi> <hi type="italic">years old</hi>, (or, <hi type="italic">to the borders thereof, even as an</hi> <hi type="italic">heifer</hi>.) — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42784" type="x-p"/> FT234 “Jonathan translates the word <foreign xml:lang="he">בריחה</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">berechahh</hi>,) as if it had been written <foreign xml:lang="he">בורחים</foreign> (<hi type="italic">borachim</hi>,) that is, <hi type="italic">those who</hi> <hi type="italic">flee</hi>; so that the meaning will be, ‘Some of them shall <hi type="italic">flee</hi>, in order to preserve themselves, <hi type="italic">even to Zoar</hi>, as Lot, their father, once did, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.19.23">Genesis 19:23</reference>,) who fled to <hi type="italic">Zoar</hi>.’” — <hi type="italic">Jarchi</hi><div eID="gen42784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42785" type="x-p"/> FT235 <hi type="italic">Therefore the abundance they have gotten</hi>. — Eng. Ver. <hi type="italic">Therefore the substance which they have saved</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Stock</hi> <hi type="italic">The riches which they have gained</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Lowth</hi><div eID="gen42785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42786" type="x-p"/> FT236 For <hi type="italic">the cry is gone round about the borders of Moab</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42787" type="x-p"/> FT237 “Alluding to the name <hi type="italic">Dimon</hi>, which signifies <hi type="italic">Bloodtown</hi>.” — <hi type="italic">Rosenmuller</hi><div eID="gen42787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42788" type="x-p"/> FT238 <hi type="italic">For I will bring more</hi> (Heb. <hi type="italic">additions</hi>) <hi type="italic">upon</hi> <hi type="italic">Dimon</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42789" type="x-p"/> FT239 “This I take to be <hi type="italic">the plague of lions</hi>, recorded in <reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.25">2 Kings 17:25</reference>, which afflicted the new inhabitants of the land of Israel, and the remnant of the Moabites, suffered to continue there by Shalmanezer. Other interpretations are proposed; but it is best, in obscure local prophecies, to adhere to the little light afforded by the records of the times.” — <hi type="italic">Stock</hi><div eID="gen42789" type="x-p"/> </note> So far as relates to the words, some pass by the Hebrew noun <foreign xml:lang="he">בית</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">baith</hi>;) but as it signifies <hi type="italic">a house</hi> and <hi type="italic">a temple</hi>, it is probable that it was the word commonly used for <hi type="italic">a temple</hi>, as in many other passages <hi type="italic">the</hi> <hi type="italic">house of God</hi> means <hi type="italic">the temple</hi> <note n="237"> <div sID="gen42790" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42790" type="x-p"/> </note> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.19 Bible:Exod.34.26 Bible:Deut.23.18 Bible:Josh.9.23">Exodus 23:19, 34:26; Deuteronomy 23:18; Joshua 9:23</reference>.) By representing the Moabites as bowing down before their idols, he at the same time condemns their superstition in worshipping their idol Chemosh, as may easily be inferred from <reference osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.11.7">1 Kings 11:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.7 Bible:Jer.48.13">Jeremiah 48:7, 13</reference>. “The Moabites,” says Isaiah, “shall betake themselves to their god when matters are so desperate, but to no purpose; for they shall find in him no assistance.”<div eID="gen42776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42791" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And to Dibon to the high places.</hi> This makes it still more evident that he is speaking of the Temple; and it is beyond a doubt that the Moabites had a fortress remarkable and celebrated above the rest, in which they had built <hi type="italic">high places</hi> in honor of their idol. Being ignorant of the true God, to whom they might betake themselves in adversity, we need not wonder that they betake themselves to an idol, in conformity to their ordinary custom. By doing this they increased their misery, and brought upon themselves an accumulation of all distresses; for they inflamed the wrath of God still more by those very means which they considered to be fitted for appeasing his wrath. He therefore wished to state more plainly the condition of the ungodly, who have no refuge in adversity; for as to those remedies which they think will be adapted to their diseases, nothing can be more destructive to them, since they excite more and more the Lord’s indignation.<div eID="gen42791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42792" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Moab shall howl over Nebo and over Medeba.</hi> <hi type="italic">Nebo</hi> also was one of the cities of the <hi type="italic">Moabites</hi>. The Prophet has already named two of them, <hi type="italic">Ar</hi> and <hi type="italic">Kir</hi>; he now adds a third, <hi type="italic">Nebo</hi>; and lastly he mentions a fourth, <hi type="italic">Medeba</hi>; as if he had said that this destruction would not only seize the extremities of that country, but would reach its inmost recesses, so that not one corner could be exempted.<div eID="gen42792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42793" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">On every head.</hi> Every nation has its peculiar ceremonies to denote mourning or joy. The Italians and other western nations allowed the hair and beard to grow when they were in mourning; and hence arose the phrase, <hi type="italic">to lengthen the beard</hi>. On the other hand, the eastern nations shaved the head and beard, which they reckoned to be ornamental; and when they reversed their ordinary custom, that was a token of mourning. <note n="238"> <div sID="gen42794" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42794" type="x-p"/> </note> Nothing else therefore is meant than that the condition of the whole kingdom will be so mournful, that the indications of mirth will be laid aside, and all will wear the tokens of grief and lamentation.<div eID="gen42793" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.15.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42775" osisID="Isa.15.2" type="section"/>
entries.2a8d686b4d9ed71ea7b93849ec57d8e88ab531bd: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.15.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.15.3" sID="gen42795" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42796" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> <hi type="italic">In his streets.</hi> <note n="239"> <div sID="gen42797" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42797" type="x-p"/> </note> He proceeds with the same subject, describing more fully the tokens of mourning, in which the eastern nations abound more than others; for, having quicker understandings and keener feelings, they express their emotions by outward signs more than others do, who, being slower in apprehension, are likewise slower in movement and gesture. It was no doubt faulty in them that they indulged in so many ceremonies and gesticulations; but the Prophet spoke of them as what was known and common, only for the purpose of describing the grief which would follow the desolation of that country.<div eID="gen42796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42798" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Every one shall howl and descend to weeping.</hi> <note n="240"> <div sID="gen42799" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42799" type="x-p"/> </note> It was with good reason that he added this description; for we are never moved by predictions, unless the Lord place them, as it were, before our eyes. Lest the Jews should think that these matters might be lightly passed by, when he described that destruction, he determined to mention also <hi type="italic">mourning, weeping, and howling</hi>, that they might see almost with their own eyes those events which appear to be incredible, for the Moabites were at that time in a state of profound peace, and believers had the more need of being confirmed, that they might not call this prophecy in question. By the same means he points out the despair to which unbelievers are liable in adversity, for the support on which they rely is insecure.<div eID="gen42798" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.15.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42795" osisID="Isa.15.3" type="section"/>
entries.6b32119f13e72ac81b740257de902f04ed1230a9: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.15.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.15.4" sID="gen42800" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4.</hi> <hi type="italic">And Heshbon shall cry, and Elealeh.</hi> Here he names other cities; for his design is to bind up, as it were, in a bundle all the cities of that country, that they may be involved in the general destruction; as if he had said, that none at all shall be exempted.<div eID="gen42801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42802" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Therefore the light-armed soldiers of Moab shall howl</hi>. Though <foreign xml:lang="he">על כן</foreign> (<hi type="italic">gnal ken</hi>) literally signifies <hi type="italic">therefore</hi>, yet some think that a reason is not here assigned; but that is of little importance. The Prophet shows that there will be none that does not <hi type="italic">howl</hi>; for he declares that the bold and courageous shall mourn. Next he adds, <hi type="italic">the soul of every one shall howl to him.</hi> <note n="241"> <div sID="gen42803" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42803" type="x-p"/> </note> Every one shall be so engrossed with his own grief, that he will not think of his neighbors.<div eID="gen42802" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.15.4" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42800" osisID="Isa.15.4" type="section"/>
entries.d9ffdf602456e9610cac5860a863a23c0ea9af96: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.15.5" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.15.5" sID="gen42804" type="section"/><p/> <div sID="gen42805" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">5.</hi><hi type="italic"> My heart shall cry out for Moab.</hi> At length he assumes the character of a mourner. But it may be thought to be strange and inconsistent in him to bewail the calamity of the Moabites; for he ought rather to have lamented the destruction of the Church, and to have rejoiced at the ruin of her enemies. It is customary with the prophets, however, to assume in this manner the character of those whose calamities they foretell, and thus to exhibit their condition, as it were, on a stage; by which means they produce a stronger impression than if they delivered their instruction in a direct form. Yet there can be no doubt that the prophets shuddered at the judgments of God, even against the wicked; though the meaning which I have stated is simpler and more appropriate, and may easily be inferred from frequent usage.<div eID="gen42805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42806" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">His fugitives to Zoar,</hi> <note n="242"> <div sID="gen42807" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42807" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic">a heifer of three years old.</hi> He calls them <hi type="italic">fugitives</hi> who shall escape from it; for he means that those who shall escape from Moab will come even <hi type="italic">to Zoar</hi> <note n="243"> <div sID="gen42808" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42808" type="x-p"/> </note> Now, he compares <hi type="italic">Zoar</hi> to <hi type="italic">a heifer of three years old</hi>, which is in full vigor, and has not felt the pangs of birth, or toil, or the yoke, but revels in the buoyancy of mirth and wantonness. When men are hard pressed by an invading army, they flee to cities which have not been attacked, and which appear to be the farthest removed from danger. Such was <hi type="italic">Zoar</hi>, for it had never been attacked by enemies.
